Entertainment.title: Charli xcx, Reading Festival review – Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche would have loved it
Entertainment.text:
“Time itself is a circle,” as the rock’n’roll philosopher Nietzsche once said, accurately foreshadowing Charli xcx’s only UK festival appearance this summer. Like her performance on Glastonbury’s Other Stage last year – a pyrotechnic farewell to the puke-green reign of Brat – Charli’s Reading and Leeds appearance is a not-quite-headline slot that also follows a rowdy set from grime don Skepta.

Yet in the past 14 months, everything else in Charli’s pop factory has undergone a hard reset. She’s released two albums – a grandiose, gothic soundtrack to Emerald Fennell’s adaptation of Wuthering Heights, and last month’s high-concept Music, Fashion, Film, an album of raw, glitching micro-rock, with guitars shredded into Tetris-like pieces, and fitted with lacerating lyrics about shopping, egotism and mortality. She’s also launched an acting career, thrown a big fat celebrity wedding and, somewhere along the way, found time to rehearse her biggest, most vertiginous show to date.

Most of the new album gets an airing, starting with mission statement single Rock Music – a hard pivot away from Brat’s all-night rave energy and an ode to Charli’s on-stage urge to self-destruct: “I’m really banging my head / I’m really hurting my neck / The nerve damage is real.” Backed by a live band (with guitar, bass and drums played by the kind of underfed, skinny-trousered men who ruled these stages circa 2006) Charli rattles through Yeah, her pocket-sized take on Song 2, and shopaholic reckoning Card Declined, during which she’s joined by a huge cast of dancer-slash-models prowling a three-storey scaffolding set.

Her rotation of outfits is another daring homage to the late ‘00s – glittery blazer over push-up bra and fishnets; ripped T-shirt dress with low-slung belt – and the mood board is tightly curated, with video screens stuck on the same monochrome palette as every outfit and image from this era, including the album’s black-and-white cover, featuring three totemic males of music, fashion and film: John Cale (whose disembodied voice heralds a tense rendition of their claustrophobic duet, House), Marc Jacobs and Martin Scorsese. Pretentious? Just a bit. But Nietzsche, I reckon, would have got on board with it – Charli’s current pop era is basically a cosmic battle between her ego and her vulnerabilities, all watched over by serious Big Dick Energy.

Charli’s crowd are less debauched than her “365 party girl” reputation suggests, but they save their energy for a speed run of Brat’s biggest hits, including Von Dutch and girly smut fest Guess, where knickers fall from the sky like elasticated manna. There’s not much time to dig into her deep catalogue of future-facing pop, but she satisfies the hardcore – like the young man next to me who saw the Brat tour 24 times – with Track 10, a shirt-tearing favourite from 2017’s Pop 2.

The end of the show circles back to new songs, including the hilariously arch “B side” Playboy Bunny, sung on one note like a coquettish Joey Ramone: “All my music sounds the same / Well, that’s because I made it”. There’s a set from Fontaines D.C. still to come, but Charli makes it tricky for the headliners to follow her closing flourish on Nothing Lasts Forever, a morbid reflection on “the crushing highs and lows of ego”, which fades out with director David Cronenberg’s voice on a loop, reminding us of the fate of even the greatest artists – “They are dead, they are gone / Nothing lasts for ever” – as Charli and her dancers stand rigid, staring into the distance. No stage banter, no compromise – just an absolute commitment to the bit.

BreakingNewsTab.title: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv weapons depot
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Thirty-seven people have died and almost 400 have been evacuated after a Russian drone strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area on the outskirts of Kyiv.

The strike caused shells, mines and drones to detonate late on Friday, triggering a blast that damaged nearby properties including a care home for the elderly and disabled, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

He said the storage site "definitely shouldn't have been there" and that an investigation had been launched into "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people".

The attack is the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in recent months, prompting renewed anger.

Four children are among the 42 people injured in Friday night's explosion, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko, with a rescue operation ongoing at the site, in the Bucha district, on Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in Myla, a village to the west of the Ukrainian capital, holding "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles".

"Everything is completely damaged," local resident Liubov Pavlenko, 45, told the BBC after inspecting his home.

"There are cracks all around the entire perimeter, and cracks around the windows. Basically, the structural integrity has been compromised."

Zelensky said the decision to store explosives in the village was "absolutely unacceptable", adding: "Criminal proceedings have been opened on charges of official negligence."

The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general earlier said it was reviewing the "legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials" near residential buildings in Myla.

It said the "actions of officials who made the relevant decisions" would also be investigated.

However, Zelensky earlier stated that "there are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas", adding "appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn".

He referenced the strike on an ammunition warehouse in Vyshneve in July, which caused a secondary detonation that killed nine, injured dozens more and damaged more than 280 homes.

Friday night's explosion has raised fresh questions about why munitions were being stored so close to people's homes, especially given the regularity of Russian aerial attacks.

"The authorities, the Ministry of Defence - why was this allowed at the depots, in a place where there used to be food?" Borys Daniyluk, 61, said.

"Why were ammunition and weapons stored there, next to a populated village? There are no words, just emotions."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.

Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.

"May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."

South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.

"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

On social media, author Andrew Ollerton said he was "reeling" after seeing the incident.

"My wife Charlotte and I were walking just a few paces behind when a huge overhead sign came crashing down on the people in front of us," he said.

"We rushed with others to lift the sign off them and then administered first aid with others as best we could until the paramedics arrived."

Judah Martin, from Kent, was at the event and said he saw vehicles "speeding" towards the area where the incident happened before campers were told to return to their tents "immediately".

"As we had no internet connection, we were unable to access information, except that word spread that there were serious injuries due to a falling sign," the 20-year-old told Your Voice.

"The sign in question was a huge wooden sign on the top of a hill which we walked under earlier that day."

Rayanne Walters celebrated her birthday on Friday at the festival and spent the night before returning to her home in London on Saturday.

"You could hear people crying in the middle of the night," she said.

"People were crying because we were just so upset."

Jessica Schuffenhauer travelled from Leipzig in Germany for the festival.

She said people were "united" inside after the incident as they sang and prayed together.

Carla Diamond, from Hertfordshire, said: "We've got lots of friends here and it was really uncertain not knowing who was directly involved and if people were safe."

Peter Heard, from Wiltshire, said him and his friends were "all pretty bewildered" after the incident and "a little dazed".

Christian parent support charity ParentFuel said its people at the festival were all safe.

"We cannot praise the BCF (Big Church Festival) team enough for the way things have been handled," they said on social media on Saturday morning.

"We are currently sat in the volunteer tent with a brew in hand, worship music being played and the warmth of chatter around us."

The charity said it was a "freak accident".

"Life is so precious and so, so short. This weekend brought that ever closer for us all," they added.

Sussex Police is urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.

The Health and Safety Executive and local authority had also been informed, the force added.

Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell

BreakingNewsTab.title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.

"I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times.

Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."

The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.

A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".

Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again.

"We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added.

A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.

The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.

Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London".

Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour".

He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame".

Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."

The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.

The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The former Duchess of York is expected "back in the UK shortly", a source close to her has told the BBC.

Sarah Ferguson was thought to be living abroad after she was forced to move out of Royal Lodge in Windsor, which she shared with her ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, in October.

Ferguson was last seen in public at the Duchess of Kent's funeral the previous month.

She is reportedly renting out a gated property in the Home Counties, according to the Sun newspaper.

Mountbatten-Windsor and Ferguson relinquished their royal titles following increased scrutiny and revelations surrounding their links to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.

It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.

She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.

In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family."

A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.

Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.

The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.

Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.

Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.

The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.

Except here, in China.

Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.

It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.

Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.

But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.

Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.

China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.

That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.

There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.

On Saturday, new footage from Chinese state media showed rescue teams wandering in a wasteland of mud and rock while calling out to anyone trapped.

But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.

We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.

As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.

On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".

Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.

Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.

Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.

This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.

China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.

The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.

The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.

It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.

Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.

Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.

A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.

The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".

It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.

That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.

The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.

There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.

They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.

Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.

Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Nepal flood devastation revealed in satellite imagery
BreakingNewsTab.text:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit.

A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared.

The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud.

One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from.

A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away.

Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river.

Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building.

Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded.

Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video.

The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley.

At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed.

This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.

But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.

Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

BreakingNewsTab.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.

She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.

Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers.

"We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said.

"Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."

Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China.

Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry.

The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.

He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."

Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday.

"It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.

Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".

The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.

Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.

She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit.

"We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.

Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods.

"My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said.

"They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."

Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.

He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.

The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated."

Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent.

Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

"My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.

A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing.

Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.

Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal.

"Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time.

"Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."

Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit.

Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.

"We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added.

"The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."

Tatajana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she has not been able to contact her sister who was near the Nepal-Tibet border when devastating flash flooding hit.

She said the last known location of her sister Julija Jakovicka was in the border area an hour before the flash floods struck.

"Then there is no more news," she told the BBC.

Phillips said her sister, a mother-of-two living in Germany, was in the country for a yoga and meditation retreat.

"We are terribly worried," added Phillips' husband Ben. "We just know where they were and that's really tough."

A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.

Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.

His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.

She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.

Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.

The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.

Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.

Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

The company's travel logs which were shared with PA Media.

Four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu.

Preliminary information suggested it was caused by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said additional analysis indicated "the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide."

It said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event caused by a "glacial collapse and debris flow" occurred near the border at 08:37 local time (03:52GMT) on Wednesday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government following the floods, saying it was a "very distressing and devastating situation".

He had previously urged Britons in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

Speaking on Thursday, King Charles said he and the Queen were "heartbroken" and sent their "most profound sympathy" to those affected.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.

The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.

The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."

A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.

The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.

Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.

"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.

"I enjoyed going over."

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.

In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".

The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.

Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.

Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.

But she has never spoken publicly about what she saw.

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.

Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.

"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.

As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.

Then, things fell apart in a dramatic and unexpected way.

Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.

"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.

His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.

But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.

The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.

Bayoumi presented himself as an ordinary family man.

The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.

Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.

"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.

But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.

In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.

The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.

In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.

"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.

The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.

"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.

Ratchford had rules. It was a quick no.

But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.

Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.

The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.

Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.

The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

Holly saw the pair repeatedly in the following few months.

"I would have cookies and tea with them. It wasn't like they were just someone that came into the office and rented from us," she says.

Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.

But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.

Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"

"And I went, 'What?'"

Then, the FBI came knocking.

On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.

She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 families' lawsuit, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

The FBI found that Bayoumi's contacts had helped Hazmi and Mihdhar obtain California driver's licences, apply to flight schools, receive Middle Eastern wire transfers, and even arrange dental treatment.

The FBI agents wanted to interview Bayoumi. They traced him more than 5,000 miles (8,000km) to the UK, to Birmingham, where he had moved just before 9/11.

On 21 September 2001, he was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch and detectives began questioning him.

Seeming unflustered, and at times indignant, Bayoumi initially denied knowing any of the hijackers.

He said he had often helped people find accommodation but, when detectives pressed him, said he could not remember the names of anyone for whom he had guaranteed an apartment.

A day later, he said he remembered helping two individuals, "Nawaf" and "Khalid" - the first names of Hazmi and Mihdhar.

He admitted they were the only two people to whom he had given this level of support.

Bayoumi claimed he had met the pair in Los Angeles, after briefly overhearing them speaking Arabic in a restaurant. He said he had told them that if they ever went to San Diego, he could help them.

The next day, he told the British detectives, the men had shown up at his local mosque in San Diego saying they needed a place to live. He had then driven them back to Parkwood to see Ratchford about finding them an apartment.

After Hazmi and Mihdhar had moved in, Bayoumi said he had avoided them. He said he had left town, and that when he returned, he found they had moved on.

In his account, Bayoumi's association with the future hijackers was fleeting. But his story does not match Ratchford's version of events.

"I know that's what he said, and I know that's bullshit," she says.

Before he brought the hijackers to her office, Ratchford says Bayoumi had asked her several times about finding an apartment for two people.

"I would tell him what would be available and he'd be like, 'oh no, no, I want that one'," she says. "He wanted something near him, and he was hoping for the least expensive place."

She also contradicts Bayoumi's claim that he hardly saw the hijackers after he secured their apartment, explaining that she had seen them together over the weeks that followed. On one occasion, the three of them had come to her office for tea and cookies.

"It's not like he just found them an apartment and never talked to them again," she says, adding that the three men "were definitely friendly".

Ratchford also told the FBI that when the hijackers had fallen behind with paying their rent, Bayoumi had paid it.

The Met Police held Bayoumi for seven days - the maximum at the time. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) decided not to extradite him to face charges.

On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.

Ratchford is still stunned.

"I can't believe he got away," she says.

Bayoumi left the UK for Saudi Arabia in August 2002.

Two years later, he was, in effect, cleared when the US's 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the attacks - concluded he was "obliging and gregarious" and "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". The FBI had not shown the Commission all the evidence it had gathered - and declined to comment when the BBC asked about this.

Meanwhile, the 9/11 families had started their attempts to pursue him through the courts, adding him as a defendant to their $1tn suit against various individuals, companies and governments for allegedly supporting al-Qaeda.

For years, the families campaigned for the FBI's investigation to be declassified. The wait was agonisingly slow, but since 2018 tens of thousands of pages of documents have been released to the New York court and via a presidential order signed by Joe Biden - including the FBI's interviews with Holly Ratchford.

In August last year, having considered the entire body of evidence, the judge in the 9/11 families' legal case said the evidence did not support the conclusion that Bayoumi had been "just an innocent participant".

Judge George B Daniels also noted later in his judgement that there was "a reasonable inference that all the apartment-related assistance he [Bayoumi] provided for the hijackers was not just acts of a good Samaritan, but rather that he was following" instructions from the Saudi government.

Saudi Arabia denies any involvement in 9/11 and has consistently argued that Omar al-Bayoumi was not a Saudi agent and did not have any involvement or foreknowledge of the attacks. It maintains that, under US law, it has sovereign immunity - official exemption of a ruler or state from certain types of civil suit and criminal prosecution - and that the case should be struck out.

The case is now with the US Court of Appeal, which will hear oral arguments in October.

9/11 was a catastrophe that wrought personal trauma on tens of thousands of people - the families of the victims, the survivors, first responders and witnesses.

For Holly Ratchford, all the certainties and securities of her years at Parkwood came to an abrupt end.

Nothing was as it had seemed.

"I know a lot of peoples' lives changed immediately during 9/11. For me, within a week or two, my life, my ideals, my beliefs, everything changed so quickly. It was like a flip of a switch," she says.

"I felt so stupid. I trusted and I cared about people that did bad things. I don't ever want to be as blindsided as I was by them not being who they said they were."

Soon after 9/11, Ratchford quit Parkwood, property management, and the big city.

She moved first to the beach, then to a reservation, and later, to the middle of nowhere - all in an effort to escape the feeling she was being tricked.

Ratchford kept to herself, she tells me, interacting only with people she absolutely trusted.

"9/11 made me afraid of people," she says.

"Now I just prefer to be away from people that might be lying about who they are. You can't keep a secret when you live in a small town and that makes me feel more safe. I like being in a place where I can trust people."

But even as she has sought to escape further and further from the outside world, she is haunted by questions about what happened at Parkwood.

"Part of me wonders if there's something I could have done if I was more strict," she says.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she...

BreakingNewsTab.title: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say
BreakingNewsTab.text:
As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month.

What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen.

Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues.

It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary.

Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future.

"I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News.

"The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria."

When he fronted the launch of the alert system in April 2023, he says it was intended for as narrow a geographic area as possible where the threat to life is imminent.

The government's own webpage, external for emergency alerts says they are only sent for "life-threatening emergencies", listing wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms.

Two national tests of the system took place in 2023 and 2025, while 10 local alerts have been sent since its launch, all related to weather or flooding bar one in Plymouth for a World War Two bomb removal.

The day before the alert was sent earlier this month, 19 homes burned down in the west Midlands town of Stourbridge after a wildfire. The day of the alert, ministers say they were asked directly by fire chiefs to send one as crews dealt with 43 wildfires and 11 major incidents across the country.

The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.

It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.

Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.

"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."

A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.

"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.

The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.

"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.

But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.

He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.

"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."

His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"

Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.

"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.

Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts:

Severe weather and environmental alerts such as flood risk

Bomb dispersal evacuation

Major hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005

Coal tip landslides

When building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children.

The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app.

It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks.

Another one of those involved in creating the alert system, Nick Corney, thinks the government "missed a trick" with the wildfire alert by sending it nationally rather than targeted at specific postcodes with the highest risk.

Corney, who worked in the Cabinet Office between 2018 and 2021 and says he was in weekly and then daily meetings about designing alerts, wants a "thorough review".

He says this would look at making future alert wording more specific, such as explaining the threat to life with a link to a webpage. "An extra level of consideration needs to be put in place" for national alert versus a local one, he adds.

"You've really got to take yourself out of the Cobra room," he says.

"There's a level of scaring the public that needs to be taken into consideration."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Andy Burnham is set to come under the most intense scrutiny of his political life when Parliament returns on Tuesday.

Since coming to power six weeks ago, the new prime minister has largely been free to set his own agenda.

The timing of Labour's leadership contest meant he walked into Number 10 after the House of Commons began its summer break, denying MPs the chance to question him and creating what some have seen as a honeymoon period.

Burnham has embarked on what Downing Street called a "summer tour" of the UK, appeared on podcasts and announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

But things are about to get a lot tougher, with MPs finally getting a chance to grill the new PM when he makes a statement to Parliament on his priorities as PM.

He has taken questions from MPs in the Commons before, when he was a minister in Tony Blair and Gordon Brown's Labour governments.

But Tuesday will be his first appearance on the government front bench for 16 years.

The team around Burnham view the start of his premiership as successful but say they will be relieved to get back to the "structure" of parliamentary politics.

Burnham will know he has really arrived as PM when he makes his debut at prime minister's questions (PMQs) on Wednesday, after almost two decades of trying to get there.

A packed Commons chamber, with curveball questions, hostile opposition politicians and the biggest TV and online audience of the week will be a world away from his nine years as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

One Number 10 source said Burnham's debut would be used as a "learning exercise" to discover "what works and what doesn't".

The new PM is said to be keen to adopt a "tonal shift" at the weekly half-hour session and will attempt to bring more humour to the occasion.

Most prime ministers enter PMQs with a thick folder of notes covering what they hope is every conceivable question they might face.

Burnham likes to speak without notes, as he did in his first speech outside Downing Street, and is thought to be considering doing the same at PMQs.

His aides sound equally relaxed about the task ahead, even though the next few weeks could define his entire premiership.

One phrase being used by Burnham's inner circle to describe his approach to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and other opposition MPs is "problem solving, not point scoring".

Badenoch will also have to recalibrate her approach to PMQs, with senior Tory aides saying Burnham is a "different proposition" to Sir Keir Starmer.

The Tory leader was increasingly combative and sharp with Sir Keir, but a senior Tory aide says Badenoch "knows that when you get a new problem you need a new solution".

Badenoch has recently accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who doesn't relish taking difficult decisions, a characterisation she is likely to use again in her Commons clashes with him.

The Conservatives have identified three areas on which they believe Burnham could be vulnerable to attacks: defence spending, the potential for tax rises and the early release of prisoners.

The row around prisoner early release has created arguably Burnham's most challenging moment yet.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected to make a statement in Parliament early next week, announcing how the government will ensure the killers of PC Andrew Harper are not released early.

Responsibility for fixing this political problem was handed to Norris when the prime minister publicly said he was confident that his new justice secretary could find a solution.

Officials had been stressing for weeks that this was not an easy fix, and the prime minister's critics believe this could turn out to be an early example of him choosing not to take a difficult decision, which would leave some people upset and angry.

Norris's announcement is set to include measures to both free up more prison space and create legal carve-outs to make some prisoners ineligible for early release, but those inside the Ministry of Justice are determined not to allow the details to be leaked.

Message discipline is being emphasised inside the Treasury too.

The biggest moment for the Burnham government this autumn will come on 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey unveils the Budget.

Sir Keir and his chancellor Rachel Reeves were widely seen to have been damaged politically when many of the policies in their Budgets made their way into the media.

In response, Burnham's administration has put measures in place to try to stop those leaks and it's understood the Treasury is telling officials that Budget security is like national security.

Nevertheless, speculation about the Budget is likely to dominate the coming weeks in Westminster, in particular questions about what taxes could potentially be increased.

Burnham has repeatedly said he will keep Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance.

But the prime minister has also said there is "room for movement" on taxes within that pledge, leading the Conservatives to believe it's a fruitful topic for political attacks.

The Treasury is focused on creating a Budget that will not spook financial markets, with a senior source insisting the core themes of Healey's plans would be "fiscal discipline" and "fiscal devolution".

Healey resigned as Sir Keir's defence secretary over what he saw as a failure to adequately fund the armed forces.

It now falls to him to find the money to fund the defence investment plan, with an extra £4.7bn needed in the Budget.

Healey is not expected to set out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence in the Budget, and will instead wait until next spring's Spending Review.

When asked if there was nervousness about potentially annoying military chiefs, a senior Treasury source said you'd be "hard-placed to find anyone sceptical" of the idea that Healey is committed to keeping the country safe.

There has also been speculation that Burnham wants to weaken the Treasury's traditionally tight grip on policies across government.

Just before Parliament broke up for summer, the government said it was transferring "local economic growth policy" from the Treasury to Burnham's new Manchester base Number 10 North.

The Treasury is downplaying the idea that Number 10 North could become in effect a rival department.

Despite predominantly focusing on domestic issues so far, Burnham will also turn his attention to foreign policy, with a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron.

And, finally, he will need to make sure he keeps his own troops in Parliament happier than they were under the previous management.

Many Labour backbenchers felt that Sir Keir did not listen to them enough and Burnham is expected to be far more visible in the Commons voting lobbies and tea rooms than his predecessor.

Sources say he met most Labour MPs in the weeks before he became prime minister and believes that MPs "value that bit of face time".

But there is still a divide among the more than 400 Labour MPs about what policy areas should be prioritised at a time when the financial situation looks set to be tricky for some time.

Those around the prime minister are conscious, too, of the difficult decisions that may lie ahead.

One Number 10 source said there was an acknowledgement in Downing Street that the "public's expectation bar is high and we've got to meet it".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Bradley Barcola: Liverpool agree £123m deal for PSG forward
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Liverpool have agreed a deal worth up to £123m for Paris St-Germain forward Bradley Barcola.

PSG initially valued the France attacker at £145m, but the Reds have agreed a package worth an initial £106m with £17m in potential add-ons.

The 23-year-old is expected to have a medical this weekend before signing a long-term contract at Anfield.

Right-footed Barcola prefers to play on the left wing and his impending arrival will increase the doubts around Cody Gakpo's future at Liverpool.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport both Tottenham Hotspur and Manchester City have shown interest in the Netherlands forward.

Liverpool are also in the market for a right-winger, having explored moves for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh and Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr.

Barcola has become a main target for Liverpool as they look to bolster their attack following the departures of Luis Diaz and Mohamed Salah in the past two summers.

He moved to PSG from Lyon in 2023 for a reported £38.5m and has won three Ligue 1 titles, two Champions Leagues, the French Cup twice, as well as the Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Intercontinental Cup.

The fee Liverpool have agreed to pay includes covering a solidarity payment PSG owe Lyon as part of the deal that took Barcola to Paris three years ago.

Barcola, who scored three goals for France in this summer's World Cup, can also play on the right or through the middle and could provide cover for Alexander Isak while Hugo Ekitike recovers from a serious Achilles injury.

Speaking before Saturday's game against Nottingham Forest (12:30 BST), Reds boss Andoni Iraola was asked about Gakpo's future and said he "cannot guarantee anything", but wants to keep the 27-year-old at the club.

"[Gakpo] has been very good since he came back from the World Cup and his holiday, with a very good attitude. I hope we can keep him at that level because I think he has been very influential in our games," Iraola he said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Norwegians are grieving the death of the beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son Haakon VIII assumes the throne.

After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears.

The 53-year-old new king held an extraordinary council of state meeting with government ministers, saying he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".

Harald - who was on the throne for 35 years - died in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after being treated there for a rare blood condition. His coffin was later taken to the palace in a public procession.

An estimated 10,000 people lined the streets in the capital to see the late king go past, Norway's public broadcaster reported.

The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.

European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.

Norway's superstar footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.

In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.

"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.

"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."

At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.

Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, taking his coffin in a hearse to the royal palace.

The date of Harald's funeral is yet to be officially announced. Until then, he will be lying in state in the palace chapel so the public can pay their last respects.

During the national mourning period, flags will be flown at half-mast across the Nordic country, while Harald's portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.

All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding.

Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised.

Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.

Meanwhile, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.

Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when now-King Haakon married his mother.

Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year found that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

FinanceTab.title: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil
FinanceTab.text:
The US has struck a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, Donald Trump announced.

The US president wrote that the agreement would more than double American oil reserves and "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans".

Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez hailed the deal as one that would help her nation's economic revival.

But some analysts have reacted with scepticism, including questioning whether the deal would address long-running obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela's oil industry.

Trump has recently been under domestic pressure to tame petrol prices, which have spiked due to the Iran war.

He vowed to tap into Venezuela's reserves, the world's largest, after the US captured its then-President Nicolás Maduro in January, ostensibly to stand trial on drug charges in New York.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the oil deal "a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people". Few details were released.

"For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100bn (£74bn) in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy," he said.

Trump said Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had reached the agreement with Venezuela's leadership "through a partnership with private business".

He did not elaborate on the partnership or describe possible commitments and terms for the US in the deal, but he claimed the agreement was reached "at no cost to the American Taxpayer".

Under the deal the US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that US energy firms Chevron and Halliburton were nearing deals to invest billions in overhauling the infrastructure in Venezuela's oil fields, many of which have not been developed.

David Goldwyn, president of energy consultancy Goldwyn Global Strategies, said there was "no precedent" for the US government entering into a lease to operate Venezuelan oil fields.

It's not clear if such a move would violate Venezuela's constitution or its hydrocarbons law, he told the Reuters news agency.

"It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale," he added, citing Venezuela's political uncertainty, weak power grid, and limited export capacity.

Venezuela's interim president said in a statement that the agreement would have "a significant impact on our nation's revival".

The deal calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100bn and more than $209bn in taxes" for Venezuela, Rodríguez said.

"These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernisation of our industry, but also to our country's economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater balance in international markets," she said.

Oil, gas and mineral lawyer Alexander Kuiper told the BBC the deal could be "very significant" but expressed some caution.

"This is definitely a headline to help with oil prices," he said, but added: "What we don't know, is whether or not those reserves turn into actual investment, and how long that investment takes to produce results."

Asked how it would affect oil prices in practice, Kuiper said: "There isn't a switch that you can flip - contracts and agreements have to be put in place... this could take a long time, but it's an important first step."

Delcy Rodríguez - Maduro's former vice-president, who the US backed following his capture - gave the venture a 100-year concession to operate in the oil fields, the unnamed US official told CBS.

Trump gave few specifics of the highly unusual agreement, which apparently grants the US direct governance over a foreign country's sovereign national resources.

The deal would also appear to be wider in scope than the US-led Coalition Provisional Authority's control over Iraq's oil revenues after Saddam Hussein was ousted in an American-led invasion in 2003.

But it is unclear whether the Venezuela agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in the South American nation. The official text of the agreement between Washington and Caracas has not been published.

Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world - an estimated 303 billion barrels.

However, production has plummeted since its peak in the late 1990s, in part due to a tightening of controls over its state-run oil firm and US sanctions targeting its main economic lifeline.

Hours after US special forces captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a raid on the Venezuelan capital, Trump said the US would indefinitely control the sale of the country's oil.

He has also claimed the rights to Venezuela's oil after saying that the country had in the past "unilaterally seized and sold American oil, American assets and American platforms, costing us billions and billions of dollars".

His framing of the deal as part of efforts to drive down domestic petrol prices comes as the global price of oil has jumped up significantly as supply via the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf has effectively been stymied - spurring discontent ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

However, Venezuela's oil reserves are made up of so-called "heavy, sour" oil, which is harder to refine and used for making diesel and asphalt, while the US typically produces "light, sweet" oil useful for making petrol.

Trump has asked US oil firms to invest at least $100bn (£75bn) to restore the country's oil industry.

FinanceTab.title: Wife of man who died after turbulence sues Singapore Airlines
FinanceTab.text:
A widow whose husband died after "severe turbulence" on a flight has begun legal action against the airline.

Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was "fatally injured" when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres).

She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment.

"When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating," she said.

Kitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.

The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing.

"There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said.

"It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."

As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR.

Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.

It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.
